story.h1: We had to figure it out alone. They shouldn’t have to.
story.p1: Own Two Feet started with three students, Dane, Jewell and Marco, comparing notes. We’d all been the person people turned to for a frozen laptop, a cabinet off its hinge, a wall that needed paint, or a car that wouldn’t start. Most of the time, nobody had shown us how.
story.p2: Some of us grew up without a dad around much. All of us watched parents and relatives work long hours to keep things going. A busy parent isn’t a missing parent. Sometimes everyone’s just busy, and a kid steps up and figures it out alone.
story.p3: So we asked a simple question: how many other boys are in the same spot? The problem isn’t that they can’t learn. It’s that someone may never have had the time to teach them.
story.stillP: Own Two Feet is a student venture. We’re writing our workshops now, and seven free topic manuals are ready to read. No workshops are running yet, and we’re not booking any.
story.q1: “I was working to make sure my kids had what they needed, but I couldn’t always be there to teach them every little thing.”
story.c1: Marco’s mom, a single mother who at times worked three jobs
story.q2: “Sometimes YouTube videos don’t explain it fully, and then you have to go to a totally different video. It’s not a relationship, and it’s really confusing.”
story.q3: “I didn’t always want to ask for help because my parents were already busy. Sometimes I just figured things out so I could help my brothers.”
story.q4: “I was missing guidance in so many areas when I was that age. This would’ve been a huge help for me.”
story.q5: “Guys love to know how to do things and love to have knowledge.”
story.whoLede: Three Baylor University students on one venture team. We run the interviews, write the workshops and build this site ourselves.
story.m1role: Mechanical engineering, Baylor University, graduating December 2027
story.m1p: Two engineering internships at Halliburton. Co-founder and Vice President of Baylor’s SHPE chapter, and President of the Engineering and Computer Science Dean’s Committee. He built this site and the activities, and his mom’s words are the first quote above.
story.m2p: Dane started with the people closest to him, his own father and an uncle, then friends like Jayden S. The same thing came up every time: they wished someone had shown them when they were younger. Those conversations are a big part of why we started.
story.m3role: Interviews and customer research, Baylor University
story.m3p: Jewell talked to five people, from Shepherd S. at 14 to adults looking back on growing up without much help at home. Joseph P.’s line about videos not being a relationship is why every workshop is hands-on. Jewell’s interview with Steven S. is what pointed us toward schools and community groups as the ones who bring workshops to students.
story.shapedLede: We talked to parents, mentors and young men about growing up and learning this stuff.
story.v1h: Videos help, but they don’t stick
story.v1p: Stuff you learn alone from a video is easy to forget. Learning from a real person sticks.
story.v2h: Kids don’t want to bother busy parents
story.v2p: A lot of boys figure things out on their own so they don’t add to their parents’ stress.
story.v3p: Workshops have to make questions feel normal and safe.
story.v4h: Not everyone thinks they need it
story.v4p: So we focus on what free videos can’t give you: hands-on practice with someone there to help.
story.k1p: We work alongside parents, counselors and mentors, and send skills home with students.
story.k2p: Students learn by doing, with someone nearby to answer questions and catch mistakes.
story.k3p: Knowing when to stop and ask for help is a skill too, and we teach it every session.
story.k4p: No student is behind because of how his family works. Everyone starts somewhere.
story.ctaH: Want this for your students someday?
story.ctaP: Join the interest list and tell us about your students. We’ll email you when we launch.
